final.title: Exit plans get expensive when the workflow lives in your head
final.body:
The cost of an exit plan is highest when the workflow still lives in your head.

If you are an owner-operator, the real problem is often not the exit plan itself. It is the unfinished repeatable work underneath it: customer questions, lead follow-up, invoice logging, and other tasks that keep coming back. In the representative small-business scenario, that can feel like 8–10 hours a week, but that figure is only a persona example, not a benchmark.

That kind of load can crowd out the boring work that makes a handover easier: writing down process steps, naming approval points, and showing where the work starts and stops. AI is not the answer for everything, and it should not touch money movement or other high-risk decisions. Final approval stays human.

So the practical next step is simple: pick one recurring workflow this week, map the handoff points and approval rules, and decide whether it is a good candidate for automation before you design the exit plan around it. If it is, Bareni’s normal sequence starts with a free 30-minute diagnostic and a one-page pilot proposal; timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.

final.title: Exit plans get expensive when the workflow stays in your head
final.body:
If you are the only one who knows how the business actually runs, an exit gets more expensive before you even talk about a buyer. The cost is not only money. It is the time you spend answering the same customer questions, chasing leads, and cleaning up invoices instead of writing down how the work flows.

That 8–10 hour figure is only a persona scenario, not a benchmark. But it points at a real decision: which recurring task should you take out of your head first? Pick one workflow that is repeatable and easy to observe, such as customer-inquiry triage, lead routing, or invoice logging. Do not start with the whole business.

If AI fits that one task, Bareni’s normal sequence is simple: a free 30-minute diagnostic to check the workflow, then a one-page pilot proposal, then a paid MVP in days. Those timings are intended scopes, not guarantees. Final approval stays human, especially for any money movement or other high-risk decision.

The practical next step is boring on purpose: audit which task eats the most time this week. That is usually the one worth documenting first. No drama; just less mess to sort out later.
